messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmed, a 34-year-old Middle Eastern man married to his high school sweetheart, has worked for years at a prestigious publishing house in New York City. His life changed drastically when he witnessed his younger sister being attacked while she was home alone one evening. Since that traumatic event nearly two years ago, Ahmed’s world has been fraught with constant vigilance and recurring memories of the incident. The night of the attack is still vivid to him; fragmented pieces of memory play out like disjointed scenes in a film. He can hear his sister screaming for help, and the sound of shattering glass echoes in his head whenever he thinks about it. Ahmed had come to believe that being vulnerable was the primary trigger for such events. This belief was reinforced when he found himself feeling extremely exhausted one day at work, which made him think back to how helpless and tired he felt during and after the attack. As a result of this trauma, Ahmed is constantly on edge, studying people’s faces and body language meticulously to detect any sign of threat. He finds himself noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in almost every environment he enters. This hyper-vigilance has become so intense that it even affects his daily commute. The sight of a crowded bus can trigger vivid images of the attack, replaying over and over in his mind. The fragmented memories are particularly distressing because they do not form a coherent narrative, leaving Ahmed feeling even more anxious about what he might have missed or misinterpreted. One moment, he remembers hearing his sister’s voice; another, the attacker’s heavy breathing; and yet another, the sharp clink of breaking glass. These disjointed recollections can be triggered by seemingly mundane events, such as riding a bus, which he now avoids at all costs. Ahmed’s memories have become so intrusive that they disrupt his work and personal life. He recalls the exact moment when he was about to ride a bus one day, just before leaving for an important meeting. The feeling of vulnerability hit him hard, and he decided to drive instead, despite knowing it would be more time-consuming and stressful. This avoidance has become a habit over time, leading to significant delays in his work. The cycle seems relentless. Ahmed’s heightened sense of threat is directly linked to these fragmented memories and their auditory recall. Each time he sees someone on the street who looks like they could potentially pose a danger, it triggers a memory of the attack. Similarly, when he hears sounds that remind him of the night in question, his mind immediately goes into overdrive, scanning for threats. This constant monitoring has taken a toll on Ahmed’s relationships and work environment. His wife often notices how distracted and anxious he is during their family outings, which frustrates her as she tries to understand why he avoids certain places or activities they used to enjoy together. At the publishing house, his colleagues have become increasingly concerned about his frequent absences and erratic behavior. Ahmed’s life has become a series of avoidances and hypervigilant actions, each reinforcing the other in a vicious cycle that leaves him feeling trapped. The culmination of this ongoing struggle finally brought him to seek help, as he realized that living in such constant fear was not sustainable. What frightens Ahmed most is the thought of never truly escaping these haunting memories and threats. He hopes for relief from his symptoms, a chance to reclaim his life without the constant specter of danger looming over every moment.
